messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Your previous vignette failed validation. Make ONLY the targeted changes listed below.

Previous vignette:
Alyssa, a 25-year-old North American woman working as a bus driver, came to treatment after months of feeling as though her life had narrowed to a moving watchtower. The traumatic event she kept returning to was a military incident overseas, when a routine stretch of duty became suddenly chaotic and unpredictable. She described the moment as one in which everything went wrong at once: the atmosphere shifted, her body went sharply on alert, and the sense that she had any control vanished. Since then, she has found that ordinary stress can carry the same charge as those moments in service. On crowded routes, when traffic backs up unexpectedly or a rider starts arguing at the farebox, she feels her attention snap outward and she begins constantly scanning her surroundings for signs of danger, as if she has to catch the threat before it catches her. The same happens when she notices herself getting dizzy or lightheaded after a long shift; that somatic feeling is enough to pull her back into the sense that something is about to happen, and her body responds with strong physical reactions that feel out of proportion even to her.

Over time, Alyssa had come to believe that the trauma had taken more than her sense of safety. She said plainly that her life had been destroyed by it, and that nothing in it felt meaningful anymore. Before the incident, being a bus driver had felt connected to the disciplined, capable part of herself she recognized from military service; now she spoke about the job as evidence that she is no longer capable of doing the things that defined her. That belief has shaped the way she moves through the world. A day that used to feel ordinary now feels full of pressure points: a route with a sudden detour, a passenger boarding in an agitated mood, even the shift from daylight to dusk can make her think she cannot trust herself to manage what comes next. Those thoughts do not stay contained. They feed her sense of danger, and as she scans every mirror, every sidewalk, every movement at the curb, the bus cabin itself becomes another place where she feels she must know exactly where the exits are and keep her back against a wall or bulkhead whenever she steps off the vehicle, so she can see the room and avoid being caught off guard.

What frightened Alyssa most was how quickly the body alarm could be set off by reminders she never expected. A feeling of dizziness at the end of a double shift, the stress of running late, or the unpredictability of a crowded station can all bring back the same jolt of physical arousal she felt during the military event. She notices the surge immediately and then assumes it means she is failing again, which deepens her conviction that she is no longer capable and that her life has been ruined. Those appraisals, in turn, make the world seem even more dangerous, so she scans harder, watches people’s hands and eyes, and positions herself where she can see the whole room. The more she watches for danger, the more every unexpected noise, conflict, or change in routine feels like proof that she was right to stay on guard, and each one becomes another reminder of the trauma. In the depot, she now avoids chatting with coworkers in the break room because she cannot tolerate sitting with her back to an open space; on the route, she prefers the same seat angle, the same mirror checks, the same careful habits, all in an effort to keep the panic from rising.

As the weeks and months passed, this pattern began to consume the life Alyssa once organized around competence and service. She still shows up for work, but she does so with a vigilance that leaves her exhausted and detached, and she has increasingly withdrawn from friends because she cannot find words for why everything feels so empty. She sought help at last after a near-miss on her route left her shaking and convinced she would either lose control of the bus or miss something dangerous at the roadside. What she is most afraid of now is not only being harmed, but becoming so overwhelmed by fear that she can no longer do the work that once defined her. What she is hoping for, though she says it carefully, is to feel like herself again long enough to believe that her future is not already gone.

Issues to fix:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Triggers → Threat: The vignette shows reminders leading to threat, but it does not clearly state in the same paragraph that triggers themselves drive or cause a sense of threat in the required causal way.
  e.g. "The cues led to a feeling of danger that felt as real as the original event."
  e.g. "A knock at the door after dark sent her heart into her throat — her body read it as an emergency, even when her mind knew better."
  e.g. "Sitting in the waiting room, she noticed a man watching her from across the room and felt the same cold certainty: something terrible was about to happen."
- Triggers → Negative Appraisals: The vignette includes reminders and negative beliefs, but no paragraph clearly says that triggers lead to those negative appraisals.
  e.g. "Every time she walked through that car park, the thought arrived with her: this is what your life is now — flinching at nothing."
  e.g. "Seeing a man in the same jacket made her think, with quiet certainty, that she would never stop being afraid."
  e.g. "The sound of raised voices next door told her, with a logic she couldn't argue with, that nowhere was ever really safe."
- Negative Appraisals → Triggers: The vignette shows negative appraisals and later mentions reminders, but it does not explicitly convey that the negative beliefs cause the triggers or reminders.
  e.g. "Once she had concluded that the world was fundamentally unsafe, almost anything could confirm it — a figure in her periphery, the wrong tone of voice, footsteps behind her."
  e.g. "The belief that she couldn't trust her own judgement meant that things she would once have registered and dismissed now snagged and held her attention."
  e.g. "Her conviction that it would happen again meant she moved through ordinary days as if they were mined — every ambiguity became a potential signal."
- Threat → Negative Appraisals: The vignette shows threat and negative beliefs, but no paragraph clearly states that feeling threatened leads to the negative appraisals.
  e.g. "The constant sense of danger was the most convincing proof she had that her life had changed beyond repair."
  e.g. "Feeling this afraid all the time, she had eventually come to accept the conclusion her body kept offering: that she was not the kind of person who got to feel safe."
  e.g. "The threat that shadowed her days quietly confirmed the thought she worked hardest to resist — that this was simply who she was now."

---

Return ONLY patch blocks — do NOT return the full vignette.

For each REQUIRED EDGE MISSING — produce one INSERT_AFTER block.
Find a paragraph in the vignette that already mentions component A, and add a sentence
after it that shows A influencing B through natural clinical language.
<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
[copy 1–2 sentences from the vignette — the anchor after which to insert]
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
[one or two sentences that convey A influencing B, written as natural clinical prose]
<<<END>>>

Output ONLY these patch blocks. No prose, no explanation, no full vignette.

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
Since then, she has found that ordinary stress can carry the same charge as those moments in service. On crowded routes, when traffic backs up unexpectedly or a rider starts arguing at the farebox, she feels her attention snap outward and she begins constantly scanning her surroundings for signs of danger, as if she has to catch the threat before it catches her.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
Those reminders do not just unsettle her; they immediately make the bus, the depot, and the streets around her feel dangerous, as though the next argument or sudden movement could turn into the same emergency she lived through overseas.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
The same happens when she notices herself getting dizzy or lightheaded after a long shift; that somatic feeling is enough to pull her back into the sense that something is about to happen, and her body responds with strong physical reactions that feel out of proportion even to her.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
Once the reminder has taken hold, she is left with the thought that she must be damaged and no longer capable of doing her job safely, a conclusion that has made her feel that her life has been changed in ways she cannot undo.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
Over time, Alyssa had come to believe that the trauma had taken more than her sense of safety. She said plainly that her life had been destroyed by it, and that nothing in it felt meaningful anymore.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
That belief has made her hyperaware of anything that might signal danger, so even ordinary things she once would have ignored — a passenger’s raised voice, the glare of headlights at dusk, a sudden shift in traffic — now stand out as warning signs that seem to prove the world is unsafe.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
What frightened Alyssa most was how quickly the body alarm could be set off by reminders she never expected. A feeling of dizziness at the end of a double shift, the stress of running late, or the unpredictability of a crowded station can all bring back the same jolt of physical arousal she felt during the military event.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
That constant sense of danger has quietly confirmed her worst fears about herself, leaving her more certain that she is not who she was before and that something fundamental in her has been broken by what happened.
<<<END>>>
